claim: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) enables non-invasive measurement of human brain activity via the hemodynamic response.
source: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) enables non-invasive measurement of human brain activity via the hemodynamic response.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by the citation to foundational work.

claim: Changes in neural activity give rise to the blood-oxygenation-level-dependent (BOLD) signal measured in most fMRI studies.
source: When activity in a population of neurons changes, these changes give rise to the blood-oxygenation-level-dependent (BOLD) signal measured in most fMRI studies (Ogawa et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ogawa et al., 1990, a foundational paper in fMRI.

claim: The hemodynamic response evolves on a time course of seconds.
source: the hemodynamic response, which evolves on a time course of seconds (Kwong et al., 1992; Ogawa et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kwong et al., 1992 and Ogawa et al., 1990.

claim: The coupling between neural activity and the BOLD signal can be represented by the hemodynamic response function (HRF).
source: This coupling between neural activity and the BOLD signal can be represented by the hemodynamic response function (HRF) (Aguirre et al., 1998; Handwerker et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aguirre et al., 1998 and Handwerker et al., 2004.

claim: The properties of the HRF depend on many interconnected factors, including local vascular architecture and cerebrovascular dynamics.
source: The properties of the HRF depend on many interconnected factors, including the effects of local vascular architecture and cerebrovascular dynamics, that vary substantially across the brain and between individuals (Aguirre et al., 1998; Handwerker et al., 2004; Len and Neary, 2011; Logothetis et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The relative timing and shape of the HRF varies considerably across brain regions and even between neighboring voxels.
source: The relative timing and shape of the HRF, therefore, also varies considerably across brain regions and even between neighboring voxels (Buckner et al., 1998; Lee et al., 1995; Birn et al., 2001; Siero et al., 2011; Miezin et al., 2000; Siero et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Hemodynamic response temporal lag variation is substantially larger than many neural effects of interest, introducing variability on the order of several seconds.
source: Hemodynamic response temporal lag variation is substantially larger than many neural effects of interest, introducing variability on the order of several seconds (Buckner et al., 1998; Lee et al., 1995; Birn et al., 2001; Siero et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Advances in acquisition technology now allow high-resolution whole brain fMRI data to be acquired at fast (<500ms) rates.
source: Advances in acquisition technology now allow high-resolution whole brain fMRI data to be acquired at fast (<500ms) rates (Polimeni and Lewis, 2021; Chen et al., 2019; Barth et al., 2016; Chiew et al., 2018; Hennig et al., 2007; Setsompop et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to recent technical advances.

claim: Recent studies have revealed highly structured temporal dynamics using fMRI.
source: Indeed, recent studies have revealed highly structured temporal dynamics using fMRI and suggest that fMRI can enable whole-brain mapping of temporal sequences (Lee et al., 2013; Setzer et al., 2021; Raut et al., 2021; Mitra et al., 2016; Vizioli et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to recent studies.

claim: Hemodynamic signals have been shown to contain more information about fast and high-frequency activity than previously thought.
source: Furthermore, hemodynamic signals have been shown to contain more information about fast and high-frequency activity than previously thought (Lee et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2012; Chen and Glover, 2015; Lewis et al., 2016; Sasai et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: fMRI can achieve impressive temporal precision within regions, on the order of 100ms.
source: Studies examining individual brain regions have demonstrated that fMRI can achieve impressive temporal precision within regions, on the order of 100ms (Lin et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lin et al., 2013.

claim: Most common analysis approaches for BOLD fMRI data assume a standard, canonical HRF shape throughout the brain.
source: Despite the well-known heterogeneity of hemodynamic timing, most common analysis approaches for BOLD fMRI data assume a standard, canonical HRF shape throughout the brain (Glover, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Glover, 1999, and reflects common practice in the field.

claim: Incorrect assumptions about the shape and timing of the HRF can lead to incorrect inferences regarding the underlying neural activity.
source: Incorrect assumptions about the shape and timing of the HRF can lead to incorrect inferences regarding the underlying neural activity (Gonzalez-Castillo et al., 2012; Lindquist et al., 2009; Handwerker et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Studies that assume a whole brain canonical HRF are unable to decouple the neural and vascular components of the BOLD signal.
source: studies that assume a whole brain canonical HRF are unable to decouple the neural and vascular components of the BOLD signal (Handwerker et al., 2004; Rangaprakash et al., 2018; Rangaprakash et al., 2017; Deshpande et al., 2010; Chang et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Previous work has demonstrated that it is possible to quantify hemodynamic lags across brain regions on a voxel-wise level.
source: Previous work has demonstrated that it is possible to quantify hemodynamic lags across brain regions, and even on a voxel-wise level, to detect the relative order of BOLD responses with high temporal precision (Siero et al., 2011; Miezin et al., 2000; Siero et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2008; Sicard and Duong, 2005; Lin et al., 2018; Misaki et al., 2013; Kastrup et al., 1999; Liu et al., 2017; Bright et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by extensive citations to prior work.

claim: Breath hold tasks modulate cerebral blood flow (CBF) to all vascularized regions with minimal changes in cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen (CMRO2).
source: Alternatively, using a breath hold or similar hypercapnic challenge can modulate cerebral blood flow (CBF) to all vascularized regions with minimal changes in cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen (CMRO2), allowing mapping of vascular latencies (Chang et al., 2008; Sicard and Duong, 2005; Kastrup et al., 1999; Liu et al., 2017; Bright et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2021; Pinto et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Cerebrovascular reactivity (CVR) is a measure of a blood vessel's capacity to dilate and constrict in response to a vasoactive stimulus.
source: While neurovascular coupling reflects the alterations in local hemodynamics that occur in response to changes in neural activity, CVR is specifically a measure of a blood vessel's capacity to dilate and constrict in response to a vasoactive stimulus, and does not include the extensive metabolic and molecular factors that also drive neurovascular coupling (Pinto et al., 2021; D'Esposito et al., 2003; Iadecola, 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations defining CVR.

claim: There is evidence that while CVR is affected by healthy aging, some metrics of neurovascular coupling are not.
source: In fact, there is evidence that while CVR is affected by healthy aging, some metrics of neurovascular coupling are not, hinting that distinct mechanisms may shape these two patterns (Stefanidis et al., 2019; West et al., 2019; Grinband et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stefanidis et al., 2019; West et al., 2019; Grinband et al., 2017.

claim: Resting-state fMRI signals reflect neurovascular coupling induced by spontaneous neural activity.
source: Resting-state fMRI signals reflect neurovascular coupling induced by spontaneous neural activity (Mateo et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Mateo et al., 2017 and Ma et al., 2016.

claim: Previous modeling work has illustrated that narrower HRFs should result in BOLD responses containing more high frequency power.
source: Previous modeling work has illustrated that narrower HRFs should result in BOLD responses containing more high frequency power (Chen and Glover, 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen and Glover, 2015.

claim: HRFs with faster dynamics produced less power in the low frequency bands compared to those with slower dynamics.
source: We observed that while HRFs with faster dynamics produced less power in the low frequency bands compared to those with slower dynamics, they also showed a shallower decline in power at higher frequencies (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 1C.

claim: HRFs with faster dynamics showed a shallower decline in power at higher frequencies.
source: We observed that while HRFs with faster dynamics produced less power in the low frequency bands compared to those with slower dynamics, they also showed a shallower decline in power at higher frequencies (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The effect of HRF temporal dynamics on spectral content is preserved when HRFs are normalized to have the same peak amplitude.
source: Furthermore, this effect was preserved when we normalized the different HRFs to have the same peak amplitude (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The effect of HRF temporal dynamics on spectral content is preserved when accounting for the 1/f-like spectral pattern that neural activity displays.
source: This effect was also preserved if we accounted for the 1/f-like spectral pattern that neural activity displays (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: The time-to-peak (TTP) and full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the HRF are correlated.
source: And finally, although prior work has shown that the TTP and FWHM of the HRF are correlated (Siero et al., 2011; de Zwart et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citations to Siero et al., 2011 and de Zwart et al., 2005.

claim: Varying the FWHM had a more profound impact on the frequency spectrum compared to varying the TTP.
source: Varying the FWHM had a more profound impact on the frequency spectrum compared to varying the TTP (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: A wide range of hemodynamic response lags exists within V1.
source: Consistent with prior studies (Birn et al., 2001; Lewis et al., 2016; de Zwart et al., 2005) we found a wide range of hemodynamic response lags within V1 (Figure 2A, bottom).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A and citations to prior studies.

claim: The slope of the resting-state frequency spectrum showed significant differences between fast and slow voxels in 15/15 subjects.
source: The slope showed significant differences between the fast and slow voxels within each individual subject (15/15)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis across all subjects.

claim: The aperiodic exponent showed significant differences between fast and slow voxels in 14/15 subjects.
source: while the aperiodic exponent, ALFF, and fALFF showed significant differences in 14, 11, and 13 subjects, respectively.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis across subjects.

claim: ALFF showed significant differences between fast and slow voxels in 11/15 subjects.
source: while the aperiodic exponent, ALFF, and fALFF showed significant differences in 14, 11, and 13 subjects, respectively.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis across subjects.

claim: fALFF showed significant differences between fast and slow voxels in 13/15 subjects.
source: while the aperiodic exponent, ALFF, and fALFF showed significant differences in 14, 11, and 13 subjects, respectively.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis across subjects.

claim: Prior studies have shown that LGN has faster hemodynamic responses than V1.
source: Prior studies have shown that LGN has faster hemodynamic responses than V1 (Lau et al., 2011; Yen et al., 2011; Lewis et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The LGN peaked before both the fast and slow groups in V1.
source: We observed that the LGN peaked before both the fast and slow groups in V1 (Figure 4B), consistent with prior work demonstrating faster hemodynamics in thalamus (Lau et al., 2011; Yen et al., 2011; Lewis et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4B and citations to prior work.

claim: For all subjects there were clear differences in each spectral feature within the LGN compared to both the fast and slow voxels of the visual cortex.
source: We found that for all subjects there were clear differences in each spectral feature within the LGN compared to both the fast and slow voxels of the visual cortex (Figure 4C–F; See Supplementary file 1 for p-values).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4C–F and statistical analysis.

claim: The slope feature showed significant differences between fast vs. LGN and slow vs. LGN in 15/15 subjects.
source: For the (C) slope, 15/15 subjects showed significant differences between fast vs. LGN and slow vs. LGN
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis across all subjects.

claim: The aperiodic exponent showed significant differences between fast-LGN and slow-LGN in 15/15 subjects.
source: (D) exponent of an aperiodic 1 /f fit, 15/15 subjects showed significant differences between fast-LGN and slow-LGN
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis across all subjects.

claim: ALFF showed significant differences between fast vs. LGN in 5/15 subjects and between slow vs. LGN in 7/15 subjects.
source: (E) ALFF, 5/15 subjects showed significant differences between fast vs. LGN and 7/15 between slow vs. LGN
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis across subjects.

claim: fALFF showed significant differences between fast-LGN and between slow-LGN in 15/15 subjects.
source: (F) fALFF, 15/15 subjects showed significant differences between fast-LGN and between slow-LGN.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis across all subjects.

claim: In only 7/15 subjects was the average breath hold latency of fast cortical voxels significantly faster compared to slow cortical voxels.
source: Specifically, in only 7/15 subjects was the average breath hold latency of fast cortical voxels significantly faster compared to slow cortical voxels.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of breath hold data.

claim: The breath hold latency in LGN voxels was significantly slower than fast cortical voxels in 5 subjects.
source: Furthermore, the breath hold latency in LGN voxels was slower than expected in some subjects: it was significantly slower than fast cortical voxels in 5 subjects and significantly slower than slow cortical voxels in 1 subject (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of breath hold data.

claim: The breath hold latency in LGN voxels was significantly slower than slow cortical voxels in 1 subject.
source: Furthermore, the breath hold latency in LGN voxels was slower than expected in some subjects: it was significantly slower than fast cortical voxels in 5 subjects and significantly slower than slow cortical voxels in 1 subject (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of breath hold data.

claim: Support vector machines (SVMs) could classify slow, fast, and LGN voxels using information from the resting-state spectrum with accuracies well above chance.
source: We found that the classifier validation accuracies, both within each individual subject and on the dataset that combined all subjects, were well above chance (Figure 6)
evidence: Supported by classification results shown in Figure 6.

claim: Validation accuracies remained well above chance when training on voxels in one hemisphere and testing on the other hemisphere.
source: Following this procedure, the number of voxels for training and testing was often closer to a 50–50 split than an 80–20 split; however, validation accuracies both within individual subjects and across subjects nevertheless remained well above chance.
evidence: Supported by classification results with hemisphere-split training/testing.

claim: The overall performance across subjects was higher when training on spatially separated voxels.
source: Interestingly, the overall performance across subjects was higher, suggesting better generalization across subjects when training on spatially separated voxels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by classification results shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Regression models aiming to predict specific response timing performed poorly, with an average coefficient of determination of 0.104 and an average root mean squared error of 0.923.
source: Regression models aiming to predict specific response timing (rather than classifying fast vs. slow) were significantly above chance but still performed poorly, with an average coefficient of determination of 0.104 and an average root mean squared error of 0.923 (Supplementary file 4)
evidence: Supported by regression analysis results reported in Supplementary file 4.

claim: Absolute HRF timing depends on task state.
source: likely due to the fact that absolute HRF timing depends on task state (Chen and Glover, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen and Glover, 2015.

claim: The SVM classifier trained using the breath hold latencies performed significantly worse than both resting-state models.
source: However, it nevertheless performed significantly worse than both resting-state models (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<0.0005; per-subject accuracy in Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of classifier performance.

claim: The frequency spectrum of resting-state fMRI signals contains rich information about local hemodynamic timing.
source: We conclude that the frequency spectrum of resting-state fMRI signals contains rich information about local hemodynamic timing.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the simulation and experimental results presented.

claim: Prior work has identified changes in the spectral content of fMRI signals in certain clinical populations, including major depressive disorder.
source: Prior work has identified changes in the spectral content of fMRI signals in certain clinical populations, including major depressive disorder (Wang et al., 2016), mild cognitive impairment (Han et al., 2011), and Alzheimer's disease (Yang et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: Prior work has identified changes in the spectral content of fMRI signals in mild cognitive impairment.
source: Prior work has identified changes in the spectral content of fMRI signals in certain clinical populations, including major depressive disorder (Wang et al., 2016), mild cognitive impairment (Han et al., 2011), and Alzheimer's disease (Yang et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: Prior work has identified changes in the spectral content of fMRI signals in Alzheimer's disease.
source: Prior work has identified changes in the spectral content of fMRI signals in certain clinical populations, including major depressive disorder (Wang et al., 2016), mild cognitive impairment (Han et al., 2011), and Alzheimer's disease (Yang et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: Differences in hemodynamic response timings will alter the frequency content of fMRI signals.
source: However, as seen here, differences in hemodynamic response timings will also alter the frequency content of fMRI signals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Prior work has shown that intrinsic timescales of BOLD activity vary across brain regions and can be used to predict individual subject patterns.
source: Furthermore, prior work has shown that intrinsic timescales of BOLD activity vary across brain regions and can be used to predict individual subject patterns (Fallon et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fallon et al., 2020.

claim: Changes in the spectral content of fMRI signals can arise not just from differences in intrinsic brain activity but could also be indicators of different hemodynamic response timing.
source: Therefore, changes in the spectral content of fMRI signals can arise not just from differences in intrinsic brain activity but could also be indicators of different hemodynamic response timing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: ALFF is a marker of the power in low frequency bands.
source: ALFF is a marker of the power in low frequency bands
evidence: This is a definition of the ALFF metric.

claim: fALFF is a measure of the ratio of high to low frequency power.
source: fALFF is a measure of the ratio of high to low frequency power.
evidence: This is a definition of the fALFF metric.

claim: ALFF is limited to a relatively narrow band of frequencies, 0.01–0.08 Hz.
source: Conversely, ALFF had the poorest sensitivity within subjects which could be due to the fact that ALFF is the only feature that does not include information from both low and high frequency ranges and is instead limited to a relatively narrow band of frequencies, 0.01–0.08 Hz.
evidence: This is a description of the ALFF metric's frequency range.

claim: Using the resting-state spectrum itself did not perform significantly better than the chosen features in classifying fast and slow voxels.
source: Moreover, using the resting-state spectrum itself did not perform significantly better than our chosen features in classifying fast and slow voxels
evidence: Supported by comparison of classifier performance.

claim: The timing and duration of the hemodynamic response both increase towards the cortical surface while the fastest, narrowest hemodynamic responses occurred in deeper gray matter.
source: Prior work has shown that the timing and duration of the hemodynamic response both increase towards the cortical surface while the fastest, narrowest hemodynamic responses occurred in deeper gray matter (Siero et al., 2011; de Zwart et al., 2005; Duvernoy et al., 1981).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Vascular elasticity and reactivity change across the vascular network and vary between regions.
source: Vascular elasticity and reactivity also change across the vascular network and vary between regions further contributing to the variable timing of the hemodynamic response across the brain (Uludağ and Blinder, 2018; Drew, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Uludağ and Blinder, 2018 and Drew, 2019.

claim: Arteries are surrounded by smooth muscle cells that rapidly relax and expand their diameter in response to neural activity while veins dilate much more slowly.
source: Arteries are surrounded by smooth muscle cells that rapidly relax and expand their diameter in response to neural activity while veins dilate much more slowly (Drew, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Drew, 2019.

claim: An increasing number of studies are utilizing fMRI to study small, deep brain structures such as the thalamus and brainstem.
source: Due to significant improvements in both the sensitivity and spatial resolution of fMRI, an increasing number of studies are utilizing fMRI to study small, deep brain structures such as the thalamus and brainstem (Beissner et al., 2014; Sclocco et al., 2018; Saranathan et al., 2021; Beissner and Baudrexel, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Faster hemodynamic responses are frequently reported in subcortex.
source: Faster hemodynamic responses are frequently reported in subcortex, but hemodynamic responses in these regions are less well characterized than in the cortex.
evidence: This is a general observation from the literature.

claim: Recent studies have leveraged fast fMRI to detect rapid sequences of neural events related to visual sequence detection.
source: Recent studies have leveraged fast fMRI to detect rapid sequences of neural events related to visual sequence detection (Wittkuhn and Schuck, 2021), auditory dynamics (Frühholz et al., 2020), and changes in arousal state (Setzer et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: There was significantly more motion during the breath hold task compared to the visual stimulus.
source: There was significantly more motion during the breath-hold task than during the visual task (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p=0.01)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of motion data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no significant difference in motion between the visual stimulus and resting-state runs.
source: but no significant difference in motion between the visual stimulus and resting-state runs (p=0.431).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of motion data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The breath hold task directly modulates cerebrovascular reactivity with minimal accompanying changes in CMRO2.
source: The breath hold task directly modulates cerebrovascular reactivity with minimal accompanying changes in CMRO2, allowing for assessment of local cerebral vascular reactivity uncoupled from neuronal activation (Kastrup et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kastrup et al., 1999 and established knowledge about breath hold tasks.

claim: The hemodynamic responses induced by neural activity may not be identical in timing to those induced by a purely vascular signal.
source: The hemodynamic responses induced by neural activity may, therefore, not be identical in timing to those induced by a purely vascular signal.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differences between neurovascular coupling and CVR.

claim: The signals obtained from resting-state fMRI are coupled to underlying neural activity in an analogous manner as during a task condition.
source: By contrast, the signals obtained from resting-state fMRI are coupled to underlying neural activity in an analogous manner as during a task condition (Mateo et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2016; Fox and Raichle, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Studies that have empirically derived the HRF in motor cortex or somatosensory cortex have produced HRFs with similar shapes and parameters to the double-gamma HRF.
source: However, studies that have empirically derived the HRF in other brain regions, such as the motor cortex (Siero et al., 2011) or somatosensory cortex (de Zwart et al., 2005), have produced HRFs with similar shapes and parameters to the double-gamma HRF utilized in our simulations (Handwerker et al., 2004; Siero et al., 2011; de Zwart et al., 2005; Taylor et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The same spectral analysis was robustly replicated in an independent dataset acquired at 3T.
source: However, we also performed the same spectral analysis in an independent dataset acquired at 3T and robustly replicated our result, demonstrating that this pattern is preserved despite a lower SNR and different acquisition parameters (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by replication results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Previous work demonstrated that correcting for varying hemodynamic latencies across the brain can affect functional connectivity analyses.
source: Previous work demonstrated that correcting for varying hemodynamic latencies across the brain can affect functional connectivity analyses (Rangaprakash et al., 2018; Chang et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rangaprakash et al., 2018 and Chang et al., 2008.

claim: Changes in neurovascular function have been observed in many disorders.
source: Since changes in neurovascular function have been observed in many disorders (de la Torre and Mecocci, 2018; Gutteridge et al., 2020; Burrage et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Previous evidence has shown that the absolute timing of the HRF varies between task and resting-state conditions.
source: Importantly, previous evidence has shown that the absolute timing of the HRF varies between task and resting-state conditions (Chen and Glover, 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen and Glover, 2015.

claim: Task state can modulate the absolute timing of the hemodynamic response.
source: since task state can modulate the absolute timing of the hemodynamic response.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Twenty-one participants were scanned in total.
source: Twenty-one participants were scanned in total
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study population.

claim: Five subjects were excluded for excessive motion.
source: five were excluded for excessive motion
evidence: This is a direct statement about subject exclusion.

claim: One subject was excluded for poor performance on the visual task suggesting they had closed their eyes.
source: one was excluded for poor performance on the visual task suggesting they had closed their eyes.
evidence: This is a direct statement about subject exclusion.

claim: Fifteen subjects' data was analyzed.
source: This left 15 subjects whose data was analyzed (mean age = 28 years, range = 22–42 years, 8 female).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the final study population.

claim: Subjects underwent a total of 7 functional scans: 3 visual stimulus, 2 breath hold, and 2 resting-state runs.
source: Subjects underwent a total of 7 functional scans: 3 visual stimulus, 2 breath hold, and 2 resting-state runs.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: Subjects were scanned on a 7 Tesla Siemens MAGNETOM scanner with a custom-built 32-channel head coil.
source: Subjects were scanned on a 7 Tesla Siemens MAGNETOM scanner with a custom-built 32-channel head coil.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the scanning equipment.

claim: Functional runs were acquired as single-shot gradient-echo EPI with 2 mm isotropic resolution, TR = 227ms.
source: Functional runs were acquired as single-shot gradient-echo EPI with 2 mm isotropic resolution, TR = 227ms
evidence: This is a direct statement about the acquisition parameters.

claim: The spectral features were significantly correlated with the absolute timing of hemodynamic responses.
source: Indeed, we found that these spectral features were significantly correlated with the absolute timing of their hemodynamic responses (Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.
